description: We are a tech-driven team participating in NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026. We aim to build an AI-powered health monitoring solution for astronauts. We are interested in mobile development, backend engineering, AI, and data analysis. We welcome passionate problem-solvers and are looking for teammates skilled in AI/ML, backend, data science, UI/UX, or biomedical research.
summary: AstroCare is an educational astronaut-health monitoring Android prototype with a tested backend. The interface presents vital readings, measurement entry, guidance and safety information. The backend accepts heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, temperature and sleep records, preserves history, supports duplicate-safe synchronisation, and returns seven-day trends with rule-linked evidence. NASA Human Research Program hazard material provides space-health context for the guidance. The demonstration uses synthetic data, not real astronaut measurements. AstroCare aims to help a crew member notice and understand a change in routine health indicators; it does not diagnose, prescribe treatment or replace a flight surgeon.
details:
AstroCare addresses the challenge of gathering health indicators and making self-assessment understandable during a space mission. The intended workflow is to record a measurement or symptom, synchronise the record when a connection is available, and review the latest values, recent trends and evidence behind an indicator flag.

The team's actual Android screenshots show an English interface with Overview, Data, Trends and Settings navigation. Overview displays five vital indicators with units, timestamps and Demo labels. Data Entry lets a user choose a metric, enter a reading and optional note, then select Save & evaluate. Measurement guides explain the steps and label alert boundaries as illustrative. Safety information explicitly states that the app is decision support, not a medical diagnosis. Settings show sync and Wi-Fi-only controls. Screenshots demonstrate these UI states, not full end-to-end network or physical-sensor validation.

The reviewed implementation is a Node.js 22+/Express/MongoDB backend using Mongoose, Zod and JSON Schema validation, with shared contract version 1.0.0. It supports five measurement categories: heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation (SpO₂), temperature and sleep. A batch can also contain symptom check-ins and alert evidence. The API validates record structure and timestamps, enforces cross-field rules such as systolic pressure exceeding diastolic pressure, and returns item-level created, duplicate or rejected results.

Stable record identifiers and database unique indexes make ordinary retries duplicate-safe. History endpoints restore records using metric and time filters. An implemented proposed overview extension recomputes current status from the latest relevant evidence and returns derived alerts without saving them to uploaded alert history. Seven-day trend reports include daily points, baseline summaries, direction labels and insights. The production algorithm is deterministic Node code; it does not call a remote LLM or invoke Python in production. Versioned rules and measurement guides are available as immutable assets.

A reproducible local demonstration loaded 126 synthetic measurements and one symptom check-in. Repeating the seed inserted zero new records and skipped 127 existing fixtures. With the clock fixed to 13 November 2026 at 19:00 UTC, trends returned five metrics and one insight for 7–13 November, while overview returned a warning with two evidence-linked derived rules. The backend test suite was rerun successfully: 64 tests passed, zero failed and zero skipped; contract verification passed as well. This establishes tested software behavior, not clinical or flight suitability.

Current limits include a single demo astronaut, API-key-only access rather than production user authentication, synthetic fixtures, illustrative rules, and backend tests that do not establish Android-device/end-to-end integration. Sync batches are not all-or-nothing transactions. Future work includes secure individual accounts, tested client/sensor integration, clearer visualisation and expert review of health interpretation. Real human research data would require a specifically identified dataset and documented access, licence and processing before reuse.
